lesson_title: Molar Gas Volume: Same Crate, Any Cargo
hook_text: 44 grams of CO2. 2 grams of hydrogen. Same box. Every time.
clip_script: Take one mole of carbon dioxide — 44 grams. Take one mole of hydrogen — just 2 grams. Same temperature, same pressure: they fill exactly the same volume. How? A gas is almost entirely empty space — a few flies in a school hall. What sets the volume is the spacing between molecules, and temperature and pressure decide that, not the cargo's mass. At STP the shared crate has a number: 22,4 cubic decimetres for every mole of any gas. So 10 grams of chalk fizzing in acid — one tenth of a mole of gas — fills one tenth of a crate: 2,24 litres. More than a cooldrink bottle of gas, from two teaspoons of powder.
visual_style: Two identical wireframe crates side by side; a feather-light molecule and a heavy molecule drop in and the crates stay the same size; a spoon of powder erupts into a two-litre bottle filling with gas.
pacing: Provocative mismatch up front, quick empty-space explainer, fizzing bottle payoff.
